In its early centuries, Baoth was a genuine golden age. The dragon emperor Goldenborn ruled from the Obsidian Throne, and his court was a marvel of multi-species governance — humans, elves, dwarves, and catmen all serving in the imperial administration. His justice was swift and impartial. Merchants traveled the empire's roads without fear. The Baothian mark became the standard currency across Erisdar.

But the Shadows had their hands inside the throne. From beneath Pontus, they possessed Goldenborn himself — subtly at first, then completely. They embedded homunculi agents through the administration: Councilor Varik, the emperor's chief advisor; Marshal Korr, commander of the northern legions; High Scribe Elara, who controlled the flow of information to the throne. Baoth became their masterpiece — a pan-continental super-state, a surveillance machine. Every citizen registered at birth. Every coin tracked in the imperial ledgers. Every word spoken in a public square, potentially monitored. The Office of Imperial Harmony employed two hundred thousand informants — one for every fifty citizens.

The dragon emperor was not evil. He was a puppet, fed false reports, isolated in his palace, believing the empire was thriving while the poverty grew around him.

Then came the Demon King. Kirivis had spent sixty years studying a Hybrian tablet — and he discovered the truth. He attacked without explanation. The Demonic War lasted forty-five years, and in 421 BGD he stormed the dragon hall and told Goldenborn everything: the war itself was the ritual, every death fed the Shadows, and the emperor was no longer necessary. A Shadow in human form, Rulfred the Beast, revealed himself. Kirivis was beheaded. The crowd cheered.

And then Nethra — Kirivis's adopted daughter — detonated the Gift from three million years of war in Rulfred's throne room. The explosion destroyed Baoth entirely, and carved the Leviathan Sea where the city once stood.

The Age of Baoth was over. The world was about to learn what freedom without order really costs.
